title: AI literacy in K‑12: a systematic literature review
extended_summary:
This paper asks how artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is currently being integrated into K-12 education worldwide. The authors conduct a systematic literature review using Scopus and screen 750 records down to 179 papers that fit their inclusion criteria, focusing on school-level AI education rather than AI used only as a tutoring or computer-based learning support tool.

The review organizes the literature into two broad categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives. Learning experiences include efforts to help students recognize AI in artifacts, understand how AI works, use AI-related tools, and think critically about AI’s role in society. Theoretical perspectives include curriculum design, AI as a school subject, student perspectives, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The paper argues that much of the field is still exploratory, with few studies assessing student learning outcomes rigorously.

The paper concludes that AI literacy in K-12 should be competency-based, interdisciplinary, and integrated into existing subjects rather than treated only as a standalone course. It emphasizes co-design with teachers, the need for clearer curricular frameworks, and more attention to ethical, social, and equity issues. The review also notes that undesirable consequences of poorly planned AI adoption have received little attention in the literature, and that teacher preparation remains a major gap.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review, so it has a clear methodology and synthesizes published K-12 AI literacy studies, but it does not present original causal evidence or effect estimates. Its conclusions are qualitative and descriptive rather than experimental.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has broad relevance for K-12 AI literacy design and highlights teacher co-design, curriculum gaps, and the lack of learning-outcome assessment, but it reports no measurable intervention impact. Its value is primarily as a field-mapping and agenda-setting review rather than evidence of direct student or teacher effects.
